issues.explanation: Pain Recall implies the patient personally sustained bodily injury during the trauma, which is hard to reconcile with the trauma type being trauma to a loved one unless there was also direct physical injury to the patient. That is not otherwise supported by the profile.

Physical Vulnerability and permanent bodily damage imply the patient believes his own body was physically harmed. For a trauma-to-a-loved-one presentation, this is difficult to explain clinically without evidence that he was also directly injured.

Military Topics is a trigger that suggests a military/combat-linked trauma context, but no other trigger, memory, threat, or appraisal item supports a military-related formulation. As a standalone item it feels disconnected from the rest of the profile.

Avoid Driving is plausible for motor-vehicle trauma, but here it lacks support from the trauma type and from the rest of the profile. With no transport-related trigger or memory content, it appears to target a symptom domain not otherwise represented.

For trauma to a loved one, visible injuries is a plausible trigger, but darkness and alcohol smell are not well anchored to the rest of the profile. Nothing in memory, threat, or appraisals suggests a dark-space or alcohol-related trauma context, so these triggers feel disconnected rather than part of a coherent loved-one trauma presentation.

Avoiding work/study is hard to reconcile with this patient's occupation as a paramedic unless the trauma is clearly tied to the workplace, but the rest of the profile frames the trauma as harm to a loved one rather than occupational trauma. Drug use is also insufficiently supported elsewhere in the profile: there are no other items indicating broad externalising coping or substance-related trigger context, making this strategy feel tacked on.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study
issues.explanation: Self-blame can occur after trauma to a loved one, but this specific wording implies a direct causal role in the event. The rest of the profile does not provide supporting content suggesting he believes his own actions caused the loved one's trauma. The other appraisals are about damage and unreliability of self, so this item is the least integrated with the stated trauma type and surrounding node content.

Alcohol smell is not impossible, but in this profile it is the only trigger that suggests a substance-related context. The other trigger and memory items center on victims/injuries, which fits a paramedic exposed to injured loved ones or victims. Without any corresponding memory, threat, or appraisal content linked to alcohol, this item stands out as weakly connected to the rest of the trauma representation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Drug Use: take drugs
issues.explanation: Drug use can occur in PTSD, but here it is the only maladaptive strategy that implies substance misuse. The rest of the profile emphasizes work avoidance, suppression, sensory reliving, and hypervigilant threat responses. With no parallel alcohol/substance-related trigger, appraisal, or memory content, this item looks clinically disconnected from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, self-blame is plausible only if the patient had a clear perceived role in failing to protect or respond. In this profile, the other items describe reliving of victims/injuries, hypervigilance, and damaged-self beliefs, but nothing else indicates a responsibility-based trauma narrative. This makes the specific self-blame item the least coherent appraisal relative to the rest of the selected content.

vignette:
Tariq is a forty-year-old Lebanese-American paramedic who has been married for eleven years and has worked in emergency medicine for over a decade. He presented for psychological assessment approximately eight months after witnessing the traumatic injury of his younger brother, Karim, who was struck by a vehicle while the two of them were walking together after a family dinner. Tariq reached Karim first, kneeling over him on the asphalt in the dark, pressing his hands against a deep laceration across Karim's abdomen while calling for help. He remembers the smell of blood mixing with the cold night air, the specific texture of his brother's shirt, and the sound of Karim's breathing changing in a way Tariq had heard before only on the job - a sound he associated with the worst outcomes. Karim survived, but required emergency surgery and a prolonged recovery. For Tariq, something did not recover alongside him.

In the weeks that followed, the memories began returning with a quality that disturbed him deeply. When the event came back, it did not feel like remembering - it felt like being pulled back into the street, every sensory detail reconstituted: the smell, the cold, the sound of Karim's breath. The terror he had felt in those minutes returned with the memory intact, as though no time had passed at all. There were also gaps he could not account for - stretches of those minutes that simply were not there when he tried to retrieve them, which unsettled him in ways he found difficult to articulate. The intrusive quality of these memories fed directly into his sense of ongoing danger; when a memory broke through without warning, his body responded as though the emergency were still unfolding, leaving him hypervigilant and braced for impact long after the image faded.

It was at work that the picture became most complicated. As a paramedic, Tariq was routinely exposed to visible injuries on patients, and the sight of wounds - even minor lacerations - began pulling fragments of that night back into his awareness with an immediacy that made it difficult to function at the scene. The antiseptic smell of the hospital bay, which had once been simply the smell of his workplace, now carried the particular horror of the night Karim was brought in, and Tariq found himself flooded with sensory recall when he entered the emergency department. These triggers sharpened his state of threat arousal: he became easily startled when a colleague touched his arm unexpectedly, found it difficult to hold his concentration during handovers, and had begun selecting where to sit in the break room based on an unarticulated but persistent sense of needing his back to the wall.

What made this worse was what Tariq had come to believe about himself. He was certain, in a way that felt irrefutable, that he had failed his brother - that a man with his training, his years of responding to emergencies, should have done more in those minutes on the street. The conviction that he had permanently changed for the worse, that he was no longer the person his wife or his crew could rely on, sat at the centre of his self-understanding and coloured everything. These appraisals kept him in a state of low-level threat even when no external trigger was present, as though his own self-assessment had become a source of danger. They also made the triggers more potent: because he already believed himself to be compromised, any reminder of victims or injuries confirmed the verdict rather than simply activating a memory.

His responses to all of this had, over months, created their own complications. He had begun avoiding shifts when he could, calling in sick with vague explanations, and his supervisor had noticed. At the same time, on the shifts he did attend, he threw himself into tasks compulsively - overworking as a way of silencing the thoughts he was simultaneously trying to suppress. But the suppression and the overwork left the memories unprocessed, so that when he finally stopped moving, the intrusions returned with renewed force. His wife had grown quietly worried; the man who used to decompress by talking had become someone who came home exhausted and unreachable. It was she who finally said, gently but clearly, that something had to change. Tariq came to his first session hoping, above all, to feel like someone his family and his patients could trust again - and afraid, most deeply, that the evidence was already in and the answer was no.
